stage_description: The adult stage lasts from roughly five months to four years and makes up the largest part of a guinea pig's life. The animal is fully grown, with a stable weight and a settled personality. The owner's job now is to maintain good condition, a balanced diet, and an enriching environment, and to watch for consistency: changes in appetite, behaviour, or weight are often the first sign of a problem.
nutrition: The core of an adult's diet is unlimited grass hay (such as timothy), which should make up most of what it eats. Add a measured portion of adult pellets and, each day, fresh leafy vegetables. Vitamin C is needed daily because the body cannot produce it: supply it through stabilised pellets and vegetables such as bell pepper, or scurvy can develop. Keep fresh water available at all times and watch the weight to prevent obesity.
activity: Adults need a spacious enclosure and daily time outside it to move around. Tunnels, hides, things to gnaw, and hay scattered to forage for keep body and mind in good shape. As true herd animals they thrive with a compatible companion — shared company reduces stress and boredom. Avoid sudden changes of surroundings, which can frighten the pet.
veterinary_check_frequency: An annual wellness exam with an exotics vet is generally enough — covering weight, teeth, skin and coat, and listening to the heart and lungs. At home, it helps to weigh the pet weekly on a kitchen scale and keep an eye on appetite and droppings, so that deviations are noticed before obvious symptoms appear.
dental_care: Guinea pigs' incisors and cheek teeth (molars) both grow continuously, so unlimited coarse hay that keeps them chewing for long periods is the foundation of dental health. With malocclusion, overgrown or uneven teeth make eating difficult; drooling, dropping food, and weight loss are warning signs. Examining the teeth, including the back ones, is part of routine veterinary care.
warning_signs: Warning signs include refusing food even for a few hours, producing fewer or no droppings, weight loss, and drooling with a wet chin (a possible dental problem). A bloated belly, blood in the urine or straining to urinate, palpable lumps, sneezing or wheezing, and lethargy also warrant concern. In guinea pigs, going off food is an emergency that calls for prompt veterinary attention.
